judge_rationale: It correctly cites increased capacitance and sensitivity, but omits the key surface-area-driven reduction in probe impedance and measurement noise.

The candidate misses the key advantage—contactless, unbiased measurement of ionic current without direct electrical connection—and instead incorrectly claims SVET does not require electrolyte immersion.

The candidate gives the wrong mechanism and attribution; LECC-SVET was introduced by Saeedikhani et al. (2022) and uses finite-element-simulated local diffusion-layer conductivity instead of bulk conductivity.
It correctly identifies vibration as modulation for demodulation, but mislabels the measured AC potential signal as current and omits phase-sensitive lock-in noise rejection.

The candidate wrongly claims resolution is finer than the tip diameter due to remote ionic-current detection, whereas the reference states resolution is governed mainly by standoff distance and lateral current spreading, so smaller tips do not improve it when the probe height exceeds the feature size.
It correctly explains that higher conductivity produces smaller electrolyte potential gradients and thus a lower voltage difference across the probe’s vibration.
It correctly explains that platinization increases probe-tip surface area and capacitance, thereby reducing noise and improving signal-to-noise ratio.
It correctly states that SVET does not require direct electrical connection, enabling study of naturally active and biological samples.

It correctly identifies Saeedikhani et al. (2022) and explains that local FEM-derived conductivity values replace bulk conductivity to account for diffusion layers and improve current-density accuracy.
It correctly explains that vibration converts the spatial potential gradient into an AC signal for lock-in detection, yielding a signal related to local current density.
